[h1] The Sky Is Gran, Relinked In Blue...Endlessly [/h1]

This review was updated for the Endless Ragnarok DLC. This is the base game review. The TL;DR is largely the same as my original review. This game is good. There's a reason why I put 1k + hours in this single player game. I genuinely think it's a good time. It's not perfect, but the fact that it has, and continues to, captivate me the that it does is a testament to this game's solid design.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

This game is gorgeous. Everything about it. And it's well optimized too! Even the OST is great. This game's presentation is fantastic!

While gameplay isn't nearly as deep or mechanically challenging as something like Ninja Gaiden, or DMC, Relink focuses on solid, simple, yet fun combat mechanics. Every character has a few specific gimmicks and quirks to their playstyle, and though they lack a large moveset, it's made up for in how satisfying it is to just play them. Obviously, everyone will have a different preference, and with a roster of as many characters as this, there's fun to be had for just about anyone, including characters with more mechanical depth. Said characters are also rich in personality, and the game gives a decent amount of customization through costumes and weapon skins.

Bossfights are this game's bread and butter, being visually striking, mechanically engaging, and over-all just a blast of charm. This game is so over the top it's actually quite endearing.

"Sigils" augment your playstyle for each character, letting you make loadouts for more specialized teams. On top of this, characters have skills, which can change their role from a DPS to a healer, or a tank, and so on. Combining the right skills with the right sigils with the right character nets the best results, and allows a great deal of player expression through gameplay.

It runs great on Steam Deck. It's a little on the hot side, and it's best locked to 30fps (though it can reach above 45 sometimes), but even with lower graphics settings, this game still looks fantastic. Truly a testament to it's strong art design and optimization, for it to look so good even on underpowered hardware. The gameplay loop is also perfect for quick 30 min game sessions, so it actually fits a portable device anyway.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

GBFR is still, even after the dlc and the new updates, a very, very grindy game. If you're stuck with just base game Relink, you'll find certain rare sigils much harder to obtain, such as War Elemental+, Supplementary DMG V+, etc. The only solution to this problem is to choose to purposefully not unlock all characters/upgrade them and only focus on characters you actually want to play.

The game's balance is heavily skewed towards DPS. The devs gave certain bosses "dps checks," that, if failed, mean you have to restart THE ENTIRE QUEST. So even though there's all this customization and build variety in the game, it means nothing when you can't do enough damage to beat a timer of all things.

Adding to that last point, character balance is also not great. Some characters can win fights by mashing one button. Other's require a spread-sheet of optimized loadouts and gameplans just to get by. This isn't particularly an issue for an optimized party, but if you have any inclination to play this game as a "solo-character," there's lots of labbing you'll have to do. And grinding. Lots of grinding.

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

In typical RPG fashion, you can power-level your way to victory, and eventually start demolishing your enemies with enough resource investment into your characters. Thankfully, Relink provides the player a "Quick-Quest" feature, allowing you to play any quest in the game and be auto-leveled down appropriately, preventing you from trivializing content...if you play as a "solo-character" anyway. Relink lets you customize your party as much as you see fit, from loadouts, to sigils, to even party members, INCLUDING the ability to REMOVE them. The best "challenge" you can find in this game is to play as a "solo-character," where your understanding of the gameplay mechanics, and your chosen character, become paramount, as you're literally the only person in the party. The pressure is on. Problem is, the game still ain't balanced for this, because of the DPS check problem, so the only characters that can really do "solo" runs "comfortably" are the characters blessed with big ol' damage numbers, and as a solo character, DPS checks push your builds EVEN FURTHER into squishiness, making things more frustrating than hard (since the game is pretty forgiving with downs and revives). On top of this, Quick Quest is RANDOM. You can't intentionally choose any given quest and be power-leveled down appropriately, so you HAVE to run the best, most well rounded builds that provide enough dps and survivability, because there's a chance you MIGHT be thrown into a bossfight with a DPS check, and if you aren't able to dish enough damage, you lose.

The campaign is single player only, which sucks. Quests can be played multiplayer and single player though.

Some end-game quests are impossible solo without mods or cheats, due to quest time, or specific characters. Would'a been great if the game had a sigil for "solo-character" play, giving more damage or better defense that scales with party size.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I think this game is great, in spite of it's flaws and short-comings. However...this is only base game Relink. Endless Ragnarok introduces a few key changes and additions that addresses SOME of it's flaws...while adding some much needed QOL and goodstuff on top of it. But that...is a different review....

One of the most enjoyable action combat jrpg I've played in a while.

The main story took me about 25 hours to beat, although I was skipping most of it as I was more interested in the endgame gameplay aspect of the game. If you own the dlc, the game transitions into its endgame quite smoothly. It took me about 120 hours to "beat" the game, that is, defeating all infinity bosses. You can easily get more hours out of this if you like to take things slower or want to min-max more characters. 

The combat is very fluid and fast-paced, and it hits a sweet spot between being challenging and accessible. You can jump into nearly all content "blind" without needing to learn boss patterns or complex mechanics, and even dying a few times is normal and isn't as punishing as in some other games. Every character feels distinct and has their own playstyle with unique mechanics. The balance across them overall seems somewhat fair from what I've seen, although there're a few exceptions[i] (Yes, I'm mainly looking at you, Fediel..).[/i]

Once you defeat Omnis Zegalith on Infinity, you've essentially reached the end of the progression system. By that point, you'll have your BiS terminus weapon, and aside from perfecting summons or gearing up additional characters, there isn't much left to chase.

At that point, you inevitably start asking yourself "So... what now?" Like many games, the journey was the actual goal. Once you've completed it, the remaining content is mostly repeating what you've already done with different characters, or trying out different builds.

It would be nice to receive more endgame content past Infinity that improves the gameplay loop a bit, and reduce grind where it's unnecessary (sigil rng, MSP amount). More boss variety would certainly be appreciated as well, as with a regular endgame build the game will become simply too easy, and your biggest hurdle becomes simple dps checks.

However, this isn't a live-service game, and I think that's perfectly fine. Somewhere along the way, people seem to have forgotten that games can simply.. end? You beat them while having your fair share of fun, move on to something else, and then maybe return months later for another playthrough or new content.

There are many things that could be said about Granblue Fantasy Relink but I'll lead with a compliment. This action rpg game based on a very popular gacha mobile game could easily have been just as laden with predatory faux-gambling so you grind endless hours for your favourite character or just end up paying some cash. But they didn't do that. You can unlock all the characters in a fairly reasonable amount of grind. The game still has quite a whole lot of grind though. 
The main story of the game does not pose a real challenge but once you get to the post-story content, the side-quests you undertake, which become the main focus after the story, throw some fairly engaging fights at you. Having to grind some of them really wears down the enjoyment you have but that's honestly just for completionists. 
The story is a fairly serviceable anime plot, expect no huge surprises and a hefty dose of power of friendship saving the world but it does its job to keep you entertained. 
When I started playing and even now that I consider this game finished, I don't really have a character in the fairly sizable roster that I really like over all the others but this is purely a matter of taste. Suffice it to say, the game this is a spin-off of has an absolutely ridiculous roster, so the selection here is almost surprisingly sensible.
Relink's combat system highly depends on your character of choice. Some of them work via rhythmic button inputs, others rely on building up a meter, some others again deal big damage by building up and then spending a ressource. At least in this regard, I think everyone can find a character that caters to their tastes. The fights themselves are usually comprised of mowing down waves of smaller enemies or fighting against larger monsters and bosses in confined arenas, reminiscent of Monster Hunter or dungeons from classic MMOs.
Another thing that I find noteworthy is the pretty solid voice-acting in the English version. I enjoyed hearing the quips and dialogues of the various teams you can put together.

Overall I'd recommend Granblue Fantasy Relink to weebs, fans of beating up on enemies three times their size and people who love to grind to constantly make bigger numbers.

What was okay with me will probably be a big no for other players, this game is very grindy. From leveling your characters, upgrading skills and weapons to getting the materials you will need, it can take time, and the endgame is even more grind. 

Which is why the only bad thing I have to say about this game is that with all the grind, it should have been a live service game. I had a lot of fun building my characters and it's just sad to reach the end of the game, knowing that there is nothing else to do.

It took me 130~ hours to complete the game, do all the things I wanted and complete the achievements. It is a very good JRPG to play solo or with friends.

Some improvements i'd love to see:

- Option to resize HUD, there's a lot of screen clutter 
- Option to tone down effects, the visual vomit can be a little much sometimes

So i've just beaten the game, what happens now? 
You don't know?
That's when the game begins

An absolutely phenomenal game well worth the price of admission if your willing to put the time and effort as it can be a hell of a grind, fortunately that grind is backed up by legitimately some of the best action gameplay ive ever played. While there are some similar mechanics between characters (Siegfried, Ghandagoza and Rackham all have timing to consider with there attacks for example) everyone plays in a unique and different way to the point ive hardly scratched the surface with what each can do, in terms of all the characterisation every character has little interactions with one another in combat, and during the story mode everyone has unique lines for certain portions of the in game events, I find all the characters likable and while I and everyone have favourites from the mobile game we wish were playable I think this Roster was well put together if maybe playing a little safe.

The story/campaign portion only lasts a few hours and as best is entertaining at worst forgettable, chances are you've seen the tropes being used like a billion times, Relink isnt trying to be subversive or a parody it plays everything completely straight and I think it has a definitive charm, though I do agree the story is the weakest part of the experience though again it is also the shortest.

Hopefully the expansion allows a bit more freedom with builds, once you get the Supplementary damage, War Ele and DMG Cap theres very little wriggle room so hope theres some updates for that. Thats really the main criticism with the gameplay I have more expression would be a lot of fun.

Relink has given me hundreds of hours of enjoyment and I hope Endless Ragnarok provides many more.

[b]9/10 game for recovering gacha addicts[/b]. Many of the systems and UI are clearly influenced by gacha, heavily optimised for non-stop dopamine hits, but without the real-money gambling. If you understand what you're getting, i recommend it at 50% off.

[b]If you aren't addicted to mindless grinding, it's closer to a 6/10.[/b] The story is short  (<15hr) and not very engaging; even though you're the "captain" of the crew, you're kinda just dragged along one event after another. There are probably better JRPGs you haven't played yet.

[b]Combat is nothing like Monster Hunter—it's much faster and involves spamming flashy skills[/b], like Genshin Impact, Scarlet Nexus, Tales of Arise or other real-time action JRPGs. Many characters have rotations based on rage bars or builder/spender combos although some are more flexible. There is generally no need for precise positioning like MH, positioning is more like tab-target MMOs, be in range and avoid red circles. Some bosses have phases where they become untargetable and spam clearly-telegraphed patterns which you have to jump/block/dodge. Most fights that last more than a minute will involve extra-flashy events like slowed time and chained ultimates. Overall I think the combat looks and feels great, but some will find it annoying or repetitive.

The quest system is the only thing that is similar to MH but more streamlined. Simpler menus, fewer buttons needed, fewer unskippable timers, repeat quests from end screen. MH could learn a thing or two about removing bad friction from UI instead of removing good friction from gameplay.

Gear upgrading is again gacha-like, not MH. Tiers are bloated; instead of a meaningful difference from a weapon +1 to +2, you always upgrade by 10's or more (e.g. from +10 to +20) using the "add as much upgrade material as possible" button. The numbers don't really matter (until endgame theorycrafting), you don't need to carefully consider which weapon to craft or upgrade. Just press the dopamine button until you run out of money or materials, go grind the same quest a few more times, and come back to press the dopamine button. You need to craft and upgrade every weapon to unlock bonus passives anyway.

Field maps are quite simple, linear but with enough gameplay variation throughout the short campaign to keep things interesting (better than bland open worlds or samey dungeon corridors).

The 1 town and 1 city look nice but lack the charm of other JRPG towns. NPCs are repeated too much, e.g. in the town, there's a cafe NPC who you talk to, but you can see the exact same model walk past, not even a colour change. There aren't any fun interactions like sitting down or petting the many stray animals. Instead of feeling like a place to relax between quests (like MH's various bases and gathering hubs), it feels like a chore to return to town because of the respawning chests that give a pitiful amount of gacha materials.

In-engine cutscenes are well done, lots of impressive set pieces with seamless transitions to gameplay.

Story is typical anime. It starts with an established party of 7 with a lot of backstory, which is slightly overwhelming as someone new to the franchise, although the main plot point is extremely basic so you can just follow along without knowing one weirdly-eared species from another. After 100hrs I have no idea what the races are called; as far as I can tell, they are: Human, legally distinct Lalafell, Femboy, and Giant Man / Sexy Woman.

The UI for story scenes has an amazing feature I wish was standard in other RPGs and Visual Novels. There is a glossary that automatically filters words that were recently mentioned in dialogue. E.g. characters talk about X faction, if you press the glossary button, it lists the lore entry on X first.

The "optional" Fate Episodes are short stories for each character, presented as walls of text with no gameplay... but fully voice acted. The 2 that I partly read before I started skipping everything were so boring and contrived, the only explanation I have is that they are a joke by the developers to make the talented VAs read intentionally bad fan-fic parodies, then force players to play them by locking important rewards behind them.

Solid, stylish, meaty action in a richly detailed world. The main quest is a relatively short blast-fest introducing the game's mechanics, featuring some genuinely interesting bosses alongside brilliant setpieces and spectacle. Every character feels unique and satisfying to play, whether you're going it alone with a CPU team, or integrating into an online party for quests and raids.

The main story's writing is a bit hit-or-miss, the hits owing to Granblue's charming and well-developed characters, which are offset by a dump of some surprisingly generic tropes later on. The saving grace of this being the Fate Episodes and a lot of the late-game content, which expand more on the world's lore and the personalities of the cast. The latter is especially well done, and for some characters, it's clear the writers pulled from years of personal experience and inspiration.

Though maybe not as extensive as other entries in the genre, like any good meal, Relink was made with love and you can taste it. With this releasing just after Versus Rising, Granblue is a franchise I'm glad is finally getting a moment in the sun. Here's hoping the moment isn't squandered, since now that the train is rolling, I look forward to seeing where it will go.

When I say easily, I mean fights will become easy, but drops are 'puny', that's where the grind comes in. There are certain fights you will need to repeat literally hundreds of times.

If you get fed up, any you must be a saint if you dont, there are now some mods that will make the grind a little better, like 3x Fortitude Crystal drops from those fights I mentioned above so you get, say 90 total and you would still need something like 200 to level a single weapon.

Once main story is over you do all the boss fights and newer ones in similar setting to progress through difficulty, easy, normal, hard, very hard, extremely hard and then you arrive at maniac, which is where things actually get harder but not for long as you will be gearing your characters. Then comes Proud difficulty and infamous Bahamut after like 15 fights which you will need to farm to get "Terminus" weapons, the most powerful weapons that you will need to awaken and level on top of getting to 150.

That's probably where you will spend most of your time, doing the fight hundreds of times depending on your luck to get the drop for all crew.

And then, well, there is the infamous 'Zero', a fight that is designed for ninjas. Good luck with that.

A gacha-less gacha, or a singleplayer mmorpg as i like to call this game.

It has every game mechanic that i love from those type of games: kill bosses, grinding for materials, to upgrade your gear and build your character, so that you can fight harder bosses.
Most regular rpgs follow this gameplay loop as well, but they always touch these mechanics briefly.
Only mmos and gacha games are that kind of to use these progression mechanics deeply.
In most rpgs you get your gear (either by buying it from shop, or farming slightly for it), upgrade it, get your skills/moves and just maintain your character's build, but it's always very briefly done. Even upgrading is very brief there,by getting an upgrade material or money, then go to upgrade station.
In mmorpgs your character usually has a story, every step you work toward your gear, or to your leveling feels more impactful as it requires more things to do than just have money or enough stats
I played a lot of mmos and even some gachas too, but they always had their innate problems (fomo, constant meta shift, powercreep, needing constant engagement to not fall behind etc)
I always loved to build my characters, farm materials, upgrade my gear in the ways i have to put effort in it so i've been looking for so long, for a game that can capture these feelings without those innate problems mmos and gachas have

And this game is exactly that. I'm so thankful for Grandblue Fantasy Relink that it exists. It has all the things i was looking for, and in addition it has a very satisfying combat loop, fun and unique characters and possibilities to build them,it's actually insane,it almost feels unreal.
But starting with the weapon upgrading, if i want to upgrade my weapon, i not only need leveling stones, but i need to uncap the weapon further. And uncapping requires different materials in the end game. So i have to go through the process of "okay lets see what i'm missing, this and that, 3 of each." "That can be gathered from the shop by trading materials, but the other one i need to kill a boss in this mission, and it's also a rare drop" so i do that, kill it a few times, get the rare material and upgrade my weapon further.
It perfectly catches the feeling of an mmorpg in that regard, and i love it
And the grinding is not monotone, not frustrating, and most importantly, really not much for most cases. You have to put effort to your gear and upgrades, but not to the point it becomes a boring chore or a checklist to do.
Also, the fact that all the materials that is like 70-80 different kinds, all of them has meaningful uses, either for trading for different materials at the knickknack shop, or straight up needed for uncapping or forging weapons. This aspect is so rare in rpgs, i got so used to 90% of materials being useless things for selling. It's a minor thing, but it gives so much to the playing for the better (also it resembles mmorpgs in this regard as well)
Then there is the character building. Firstly, you have 28 different character to play as, that already resembles a gacha team builder type rpg, but the fact that all of them have their own unique mechanics/gimmicks, that they are their own playstyles too, makes the whole thing so good it's almost overwhelming in goodness. If somebody cannot find a character that they should main in this game, then idk what they want from an rpg. On top of that every character has at least 4-6 weapons, giving you different flavor of damiging/styles to build for your main/team mate characters. And everything can be unlocked in the game by just playing in your own pace. 
Some characters, like Tweyen, Seofon and Sandalphon's intended unlocking method can actually feel like a small event in an mmorpg, (the way how you grind for them) but without the fomo aspect, that you can do it at your own pace and even "pause" the grind if you feel like it. It's just the cherry on top of this beautiful cake.
Then i havent even talked about how fluid the game is with its q.o.l features, 
- that you can fast travel with just pressing one button and selecting the place you want to go without a loading screen (instead of dragging yourself through a map and selecting the point there)
- that if you forge a new weapon the game asks you if you want to equip it/upgrade it
- that you can redo a mission after you got your rewards immidiately, no going back to town-reselecting-reentering hassles
- that you can have a wishlist of materials, and filter the missions by which ones drop that exact materials, you dont have to remember or look it up yourself
- that you can teleport to an npc if you completed its overworld quest to redeem it
- that you can save a lot of loadouts for different builds
- that you can skip the curscenes and still get a summary of what happens in the cutscene inside the confirmation prompt

All of this, entirely in a singleplayer structured game. No gacha, no fomo, no dailies, no necessary microtransactions, everything available in the game, and you can play any time, without energy/stamina system. I cannot be more thankful that this game exist, and that i dont have to resort to a live service mmo or gacha game to get this gameplay where i'm constantly pressured by dailies, fomo and the feeling of losing everything once the servers shut down.

The game has a lot of potential that it did not realize, which is extremely disappointing. The gameplay and variety of characters that you can play is great and very responsive, every character is unique in their own way and would like to try a bunch of them. However, i am not driven to try new characters because by the time i'm ready to try a new character, i would have fought every boss type 5+ times already. The biggest complaint i have is the lack of boss/monster variety in the game, lots of the bosses are the same but just with different colors and names and slightly different mechanics. Sure they have a lot of quests, but it's boring when they re-use the exact same boss for every difficulty except they just have more HP and does more damage.

Difficulty is also an issue, it's extremely easy up until Proud difficulty because bosses will literally start 1 shotting you and missions will have 2 bosses which is extremely cheap. I love the Monster Hunter quest system, which this games follows, but with Monster Hunter, there is such a wider variety of monsters and the incentive is a lot different. The incentive in Monster Hunter is to get the Monster's gear, whereas here it's to get a better clear ranking or farming a random equipment to upgrade your weapon which is extremely boring.

The grind is also way worse than Monster Hunter and demands a lot, lots of people just setup macros so it can farm for them overnight, that's how bad it is. The first 10 hours of end game is really fun, but gets old VERY quick. Everything before end game is uninteresting as well. I heard the Granblue Fantasy universe is quite vast, but then why is the story for the game so bad and uninteresting and cliche? They have the characters and the general universe developed already, so it should have been easy to create a compelling story and integrate it into the end game better like Monster Hunter did. If only this game had more content and bosses and slightly less grind and more missions, this game could be a 8 or 9. But right now, i would recommend waiting for a sale or else you're not getting much content and it'll get boring quick. The combat, performance and initial end game carried my positive impression of the game and i would still recommend it.

[h1]I love Granblue.[/h1]

I played the browser game for a couple of years, and I've sunk hundreds of hours, both online and offline, into the Versus titles—both the original and Rising. In preparation for Endless Ragnarok, I bought two copies so I could play through the game with a friend. I love Granblue as a fantasy setting, as a franchise—I love it all.

I really, really like Relink. [b]BUT[/b] there are some serious design issues that need to be addressed going forward.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Drop Rates, Item Capacity, and Full Assist Mode[/h2]

You don't get enough MSP. The current "meta" is to pick Eustace (or recruit one through the recruitment system) and repeatedly queue Slimepede++ until you hit the cap of 999,999 MSP. You can do this almost entirely AFK by playing the first mission with Full Assist Mode enabled and then selecting "Repeat Quest," which automatically reruns the quest ten times before sending you back to town.

As you do this, your items will eventually cap out at 999. If you don't want to waste drops, you'll have to return to Siero and recycle your materials and sigils just to keep your inventory from filling up.

Normally I don't complain about accessibility features in games, especially since I benefit from some of them myself. However, Full Assist Mode removes almost all meaning from the gameplay loop. There is no reason [b]not[/b] to use it. You get the same drops, the same rates, and the game effectively plays itself.

Even reaching the MSP cap doesn't guarantee you'll fully max out a character. You need around 1.6 million MSP just to reach Mastery Level 50. That doesn't include the post-50 progression to Mastery Level 55 or the additional Offense and Defense Mastery nodes.

Including those, the total comes to roughly [b]4,200,000 MSP.[/b]

That's for [b]ONE[/b] character.

[b]That's absolutely ridiculous.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Proposed Changes[/h2]

Increase the item capacity. A limit of 999 is far too small. Players will constantly cap out on Elemental Orbs, Rafale Coins, Flawless Prisms, and other common materials.

Keep Full Assist Mode. I'm all for accessibility in games, but there needs to be a meaningful incentive not to leave it on all the time. Increase drop rates, MSP gains, or both for players who complete quests without using Full Assist Mode.
[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

I want Endless Ragnarok to succeed because I genuinely love Granblue Fantasy. Relink has one of the most enjoyable combat systems I've played in an action RPG, and this update adds a ton of replayability. None of my criticism comes from a place of wanting the game to be easier—it comes from wanting the time I spend playing to feel meaningful.

Right now, the most efficient way to progress is to let the game play itself. It's a shame, because Relink is at its best when you're mastering your character and playing alongside other people.

A few targeted changes to MSP gains, item capacity, and the incentives surrounding Full Assist Mode would go a long way toward making the endgame feel rewarding without taking away the accessibility that some players rely on.

This game was a lot of fun at the beginning.  I love the art design, and the early boss battles were really awesome.  For the first 80 or so hours, I was having the most fun with any game that I've played in awhile. 
 Unfortunately, I don't think they spent enough time polishing the end game experience, which should be the highlight in this type of game.  There's no single game killing flaw, but the combination of a multitude of issues, which all show up in the post game, gnaws away at the experience and enjoyment of the game. 

- No variety in the quest type at the end game.  There's several different quest types that you'll encounter at the lower difficulties, but at the end game it's only boss battles.  Creating proud level versions of these other quest types would help keep the gameplay from getting too repetitive.

- Progression in the post game is poorly paced.  There's a lot of things prior to reaching the endgame that players skip just because the time investment is not it.  Levelling the rank 4 and lower sigils, and leveling your ascension weapons are the two big examples.  

- Character abilities are also poorly balanced at the end game.  The game has damage caps for all attacks, and once you reach that limit a lot of support abilities that increase attack or decrease enemy defense now become useless.  Everything switches to either increasing the damage cap or dealing damage outside the cap.  You can't play as a support character at the end game, because buffs do nothing when everyone is limited by the damage cap.  It doesn't seem like they put much thought into how the game would play and balance at the end.

- The devs are completely enamored with cinematic cut scenes during the fights.  The pacing is okay when you're first clearing things, but on repeated clears it just draws the battle out for too long.  I wish they had kept the cinematics to the battles during the story missions, and reduced them for the post game.

- The Devs aren't communicating with players about upcoming changes.  The latest patch had a lot of adjustments to character abilities that caught people off guard.  Some things like abilities using the wrong damage cap were clearly bugs that would get fixed one day.  However animation cancelling is common in other games, so no one was clear if that was intended or not.  The Devs never acknowledged whether something was intended behavior or whether it was an issue that would get patched.  They just dropped a bunch of nerfs and adjustments into a patch that was only announced to be adding a new boss fight.

-So many missing QoL features.  You'll collect hundreds of sigil and wrightstones, but you can't page through them.  You just have to keep pressing the down button to scroll through them one at a time.  Of course there's everyone's favorite complaint of the transmute system.  Handing tickets in one at a time is the biggest time waster I've seen in a recent game.  One of the few announcements we've gotten from the Devs is that this will be fixed eventually.  I'm just left wondering why they didn't think this would be an issue before they shipped the game.  It's this more than anything else that makes me believe they didn't sufficiently play test the end game experience.

- Worst part about the end game for me was the shift towards all of the enemies attacks being insta-kills.  Healing abilities and items become useless, and you instead just start stacking resurrection items or invulnerabilities.  It makes most of the fights very frustrating to learn, and it overemphasizes high DPS.  The faster you can kill the boss, then the fewer attacks you'll need to deal with.  It doesn't help that most of the fights have a strict DPS check at the end that will wipe the party if you tried to play defensively.

- Trying to build more than one character is just brutal in this game.  I was able to get enough drops to completely unlock two weapons, but to do a third would take dozens of hours more to farm the silver centrum needed.  Anyone who's maxxed several character has resorted to AFK farming for this material.  If you've made a task so tedious and boring that people are only doing it if it can be done automatically, then the devs really need to rethink their approach to the end game grind.

- Finally, the Quick Quest and gold dahlia badge system needs to be adjusted.  Conceptually, this is suppose to encourage people to play multiplayer.  However, the rewards are just too little.  It takes about 75 to 90 Quick Quests to get a material that you could have gotten in 5 quests  yourself.  Since Quick Quests can place you in a low level battle that won't have any useful rewards for end game players, the gold dahlia badges are the only reward you'll earn for completing Quick Quests.  It just isn't worth your time to run the Quick Quests.  They really need to drop the number of gold dahlia badges that you need for certain items.  Running Quick Quests should be the fastest way to get a specific treasure, but you should be limited in the number of Quick Quests that you can do each day.  This would help keep casual players from getting frustrated by the grind and it would also make sure that more people are available for match making.

I hope that Cygames takes the lessons from this game and comes back with an improved sequel in the future.  I had a lot of fun with the early parts of the game, but the lack of polish for the end game soured the overall experience.

Relink turned out to be just what I wanted out of the Granblue Fantasy franchise ever since I fell in love with Versus.

I'm going at this from the perspective of someone who became a fan of this franchise after playing the first Granblue Fantasy Versus game, not the mobile/browser game. That's not out of any kind of distaste for it, it's just that I hadn't gotten into it. I mention that because I wanna recommend this game even as someone who's not a long-time, die-hard fan of these characters, setting, and story.

It's certainly converting me though. This is the type of game that I wished a lot of those turn-based JRPGs back in the day that I just couldn't get into were. Party-based action RPG with accessible controls, flashy combat, a pretty huge roster of characters who all play very differently from one another and a wide array of skills and specialties that bounce off one another, even when you're doing the game entirely solo with CPU party members. It's an exceptionally simple system to pick up mechanically, but the meat is in its progression that goes far beyond anything I saw in the simplified RPG Mode in the fighting game. It seems to be applying what the original mobile game does to an action RPG, and to great effect. It goes pretty hard the further you get into it, but I never felt overwhelmed. Challenge comes, for the most part, from bosses with insane move sets and Overdrive/Bloodlust abilities where the bosses go wild and you're expected to just avoid their attacks and wait for them to tire themselves out before you go ham on them again, though I do wish there was more variety in some of the side quest bosses. If you're only interested in the story, it's fairly well-balanced all the way to the end, including the brilliant epilogue chapter that I hope you don't skip. 'Cause it's an even better, more epic finale than the final chapter.

If you're looking for tight Souls-like combat, this ain't that. Not one bit. I love those games, but I don't think that fits what Relink is going for, and it doesn't need to try and emulate DS3 or Sekiro like almost every other game has been trying to do for the past several years. Blocking is actually useful. Perfect dodges don't just grant i-frames during the dodge, they grant invincibility for a few seconds after. Skills are on cool-downs rather than mana. There's a special meter for cinematic Skybound Arts like in the fighting game. This is meant for fun, flashy, overall simpler combat where the spectacle is the focus. What I like about this system is you could definitely go deep, min-max, use characters with timed combos like Siegfried, pick a party that suits a specific play style, expand on your build with different sigils, especially the late game ones with massive buffs and interesting drawbacks like disabling dodges and blocking for a huge damage boost, etc... OR you could just pick your four favorite waifus and play with that team for the entire run time and the endgame. That's what I'm doin'. Katalina, my stalwart, knightly, gap moe darling <3

Where I think this game suffers is in its localization, subs for which match the dub, not the original Japanese. Cygames' in-house localization team certainly has a bit of that Mahvel influence. You might see occasional [current year] lingo, which is kinda cringe. It's not too bad if you're used to how anime works once it's been twisted by Americans, but it's jarring for someone who's listening to the Japanese dub, and has been learning the language, to see how mismatched so much of the dialogue is to the subs. A "thank you" can be translated into a snarky comment. A motivational shout in Japanese could be translated to some kind millennial lingo. An explanation of a certain thing that would've been good world-building is described in not the most compelling way in English. And they actually made my boy Rackam say a "that just happened" line. There's just little things that get in the way of an otherwise perfectly fun fantasy anime romp. Not enough to ruin the game's story since I can at least understand enough of it while just ignoring the localization, but I see why it turns some people off, especially when they're playing the dub. And given this is an in-house team, this was already the case in the fighting game, and I wouldn't be surprised if the original mobile/browser game has always been this way. A more concrete example is Djeeta, the female version of the main character. She's far more consistent in voice and writing in Japanese, for both Relink and Versus, as a motivated, optimistic young girl who found herself in a wild situation and is excited to make the most of it. She's known hardship but appreciates the bonds she's built from it. But in English, it's jarring hearing this girl introspect about her long-term goals of reaching Estalucia, how she values her crew, her life link with Lyria, her respect and admiration for Katalina... while also occasionally talking sass in a kid-friendly sitcom kind of way that makes me gag. It's like EN Djeeta and JP Djeeta are two entirely different people. It's not the worst nor is it the vast majority of the game's dialogue. But it could've been way better if they didn't use the dub's subtitles for the Japanese dialogue and had those translated separately.

For as "shallow" and "weeb" as some reviews might consider this game's story, it's a good time. A lot of its depth and world-building is found through archive entries that can be picked up throughout the main story quests or found in higher difficulty side quests, as well as unlockable voiceover stories that talk of each character's adventures that I assume are from the mobile game's established lore. There's a ton to look through, just like there was in GBVS. There's a lot here that goes beyond just the cutscenes and the dialogue during gameplay, and as someone who's enjoyed that sort of less direct storytelling from the FromSoftware games, it's something I ended up enjoying even from a franchise that I had very little exposure to. I should say that this is by no means an opaque, indirect story. It's far more traditional, lotta cutscenes, some dialogue that's presented in a visual novel style like in the original game and Versus, but it's served well by all the archive entries and item text to find, some of which can even only be found in the epilogue chapter and in the endgame.

But I get it, many wouldn't be interested in just reading about a world they only just got into. You'd have to see it, and play in it, and actually be curious about it from what the actual game offers. Show, don't tell, right? Relink's certainly good at the showing part. I'd already been interested in the setting since the fighting game. Just the idea of an entire world where people sail on airships to different floating islands was already wild to me, and I wanted to find out more. Relink delivered. Its environments are gorgeous. Its world is beautifully stylized and vibrant, and all the different locations that you go through in this adventure can range from idyllic to hellish in a heartbeat without feeling inconsistent. While an open world game like that would be insanely cool, this isn't so. It's sadly not Black Flag for Weebs where we get to sail to each island freely on the Grandcypher. Maybe someday, Cygames. It's more linear than that, with the main quest taking you to different parts of the Zegagrande Skydom, and in between chapters, you can choose to spend some time on the deck of your ship or in one of the two beautifully designed hub towns to take on side quests. It's a net positive and avoids a lotta the problems that big open worlds have.

So-so localization and repetitive side bosses aside, it's wild that this is the first time this franchise went the 3D action RPG route and did it so well right off the bat. Relink was meant to be a small diversion from Gran/Djeeta's larger adventure, but I don't mind sticking around Zegagrande a little longer.
